name: quic_inspect
description: A COMPLETE, CONNECTION-AWARE TABLE OF THE QUIC DATAGRAMS of a capture, over the declared tshark's QUIC dissection. SENSITIVE: the tool declares secret_output: "required" (the whole table holds connection ids and server names as they are; the answer prints them through the withholding rules), and the secrets, if any, go through the same route as tls_decrypt: a key log given as a FILE reference (keylog_file: a job input, never the key log's text; text that looks like a key log is refused without being echoed) and/or the Decryption Secrets Blocks a pcapng carries (use_embedded_secrets); nothing of a key log line, no fragment, no digest and no client random is ever printed. Every UDP datagram tshark dissects as QUIC is one row, in capture order: frame, interface, time (the raw epoch and UTC), the UDP endpoints, and for each QUIC packet in it (a datagram may coalesce several) the header form, the packet type (the v1 table, the v2 table for version 0x6b3343cf, version_negotiation for version 0), the version, the destination and source connection ids and whether an Initial carried a token; the SNI and ALPN of an Initial (tshark derives the Initial keys from the destination connection id), the frame types and HTTP/3 stream ids where it decrypted the packet, and the limits of the row: encrypted_payload (no keys: the headers are all there is), version_unsupported (a version this tool has no table for) and dissector_missing (a field this tshark build does not have). The whole table is a JSON Lines file (mode 0600); the answer pages it (limit rows inline) and the rest is in all_results. A connection model keeps UDP tuples and connection ids apart: an attempt is the set of connection ids that long headers join; a Retry or a Version Negotiation packet ends one and the next Initial starts another (follows_attempt names the Retry link); a short-header packet whose destination connection id no long header named is an unlinked attempt and says so (it may be the same connection under an id issued after the handshake, which is encrypted); a change of UDP endpoint within an attempt is reported as migration or a NAT rebinding, not a second connection. The model is bounded (connection ids, attempts and tuples) and a bound passed makes the answer partial. UDP port 443 datagrams that tshark did not dissect as QUIC are counted (udp_443_not_dissected_as_quic): a QUIC flow on another port, or on 443 with an unknown version, is not found by this tool, and nothing is inferred from Zeek's ssl.log or any TLS-only listing, so the absence of a row is the absence of a QUIC datagram in what tshark dissected, never a finding about the capture. It records tshark --version, reads tshark -G fields of the installed build and refuses as JSON, by name, a build without the core QUIC fields (dissector_missing); a missing optional field makes the answer partial and is carried in each row. WHAT IS NOT VERIFIED: the field names and the meaning of their values (quic.header_form, quic.long.packet_type, quic.long.packet_type_v2, quic.dcid, quic.scid, quic.token_length, quic.frame_type, quic.stream.stream_id, the handshake SNI and ALPN fields, and the alignment of their comma-separated lists with the packets of a coalesced datagram) were read from the documentation and tshark -G fields, not checked against a real capture and a real build here: the suite runs a stand-in tshark, and one test runs the real program when it is installed. A misaligned list is reported as fields_not_aligned, never silently joined; but only the connection id, version and source connection id lists are checked against the packets of a datagram (not the packet type, token or frame lists), so a shift in those in an unusual mixed datagram is not flagged. A connection id is not an identity of a host and an attempt is not proof of a completed handshake. Evidence is hostile input: nothing is executed, no network is used, a listing is read as a stream and cut at 2 GiB, and a cut makes the answer partial. The tool's own clock (max_seconds, default 900, at most 1000) is below the manifest's timeout; a program still running at the end is killed with everything it started. Programs run in the tool's own process group (never a session of its own) with the kernel asked to end them if the tool dies. SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP end the tool with partial JSON and exit 128 plus the signal. A process tshark leaves behind after it exits is stopped, killed and reaped by the shared process block's settle() before the table and tshark's messages file are kept, and the answer is then partial (program_group.left_behind and a line under problems). This tool reports what tshark printed on a pipe, so a host where the absence of a leftover cannot be proven (not Linux, PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER refused) does not make it partial: program_group.unproven says so.

capture.description: The pcap or pcapng to read; never written

keylog_file.description: A key log FILE (NSS format: CLIENT_RANDOM, CLIENT_TRAFFIC_SECRET_0 and the other labels), given as a job input. Never the text of a key log: that is refused. Optional when use_embedded_secrets is set

use_embedded_secrets.description: Decrypt with the Decryption Secrets Blocks of a pcapng (tshark applies them without -o); the answer names how many blocks there are. A key log file may be given as well

host.description: Scope: only datagrams with this IP address (as source or destination)

port.description: Scope: only datagrams with this UDP port (as source or destination)

display_filter.description: Scope: a tshark display filter, one line, at most 1024 characters, ANDed with the rest of the scope (the listing is always limited to QUIC)

limit.description: Datagram rows and attempt rows answered inline (default 200 each); the whole tables are the files all_results and attempts_all_results name

max_seconds.description: The tool's own clock, 10 to 1000 seconds, default 900: a program still running at the end is killed with everything it started
